passage:
When the staffroom window broke at lunch, some boys crowded round me. "You saw Manoj throw the ball, na? He was right there, na?" I had been tying my shoe, like the slowest boy in Class 5. But they kept asking, and soon I could almost picture Manoj throwing.
When Harsha ma'am asked me, she didn't say any name. She said, "Uday, tell me what you saw, from the start." I started with my shoelace. Then I realised I hadn't seen a ball at all. I had only heard the crash.
I felt silly, because I nearly said Manoj did it. It was the wind that slammed the window.
Now if someone asks me "right? right?", I say, "I don't know yet."

qa.q: What was Uday doing when the window broke?
qa.a: He had been tying his shoe.

qa.q: Why could Uday almost picture Manoj throwing the ball?
qa.a: Uday felt pressured by the boys asking again and again, "You saw Manoj throw the ball, na?", and the repeated suggestion started building a picture he never actually saw.

qa.q: How did Harsha ma'am's question help Uday tell the truth?
qa.a: She named no one and asked him to tell what he saw from the start, so he noticed he had only heard the crash.

qa.q: How might Manoj have been affected if Uday had agreed with the boys?
qa.a: Manoj could have been blamed for a window the wind slammed, just because of a memory built by leading questions.

grounding: It shows a boy who almost adopts a detail suggested by peers' leading questions until an open question lets him report accurately.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Thursday
Parth, 8, came to see me after his aunt, Rajni, had asked him about a scratch on his cousin's bicycle. She had asked, "You scratched it while riding, didn't you? You rode it into the gate?" By evening Parth was saying he had ridden it into the gate. He told me the same, looking at the floor.
I asked only, "What happened with the bicycle?" and waited. Slowly he said he had not ridden it at all that day; he had been drawing. His aunt later checked and found the scratch had been there since the rains.
I explained to Rajni how questions like hers can put words into a child's mouth. She was upset with herself and apologised to Parth.
Jasleen

qa.q: What had Parth been doing that day instead of riding?
qa.a: He had been drawing.

qa.q: Why did Parth start saying he rode the bicycle into the gate?
qa.a: His aunt's questions already held the answer, and hearing them made the story feel true, so he went along and began to believe it.

qa.q: Which question from Jasleen let Parth answer accurately?
qa.a: Jasleen asked only "What happened with the bicycle?" and waited, an open question that suggested no answer.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel on learning what her questions had done?
qa.a: She was upset with herself and apologised to Parth, realising she had put words into his mouth. 🙏

grounding: It shows a boy who takes on a detail from an adult's leading questions until an open, neutral question lets him say what really happened.

passage:
Friday
Today Uma aunty from next door said a mango was stolen from her tree, and she asked me, "You saw the big boys climb over the wall, didn't you? Two of them, in red shirts?"
I said yes, because she looked so sure. Then she asked Papa, and Papa asked me in a different way: "What did you see this afternoon?" I thought properly. I saw a monkey on the wall. That's all. No boys, no red shirts.
I felt bad that I said yes before. "Good boy for thinking again," Papa said. "The question made it easy to say yes."
Uma aunty came back and said sorry for putting ideas in my head. Later we saw the monkey again, with a mango!
Pankaj, Class 4

qa.q: What did Pankaj really see on the wall?
qa.a: He saw a monkey on the wall.

qa.q: Why did Pankaj first say yes to Uma aunty?
qa.a: Pankaj felt pressured and unsure, because Uma aunty looked so certain and her question already described two boys in red shirts, so agreeing felt like the right answer.

qa.q: What difference did Papa's question make?
qa.a: Papa asked "What did you see this afternoon?", which made Pankaj think properly instead of agreeing with a story someone else supplied.

qa.q: How might Uma aunty feel when the monkey appears with a mango?
qa.a: She may feel relieved and a bit embarrassed that her question nearly blamed boys who did nothing, which is why she came back to say sorry. 😅

grounding: It shows a boy who agrees with a neighbour's leading question until his father's open question brings out what he really saw.

passage: At the village school near Sehore, someone had left the garden gate open, and the headmaster's goat had eaten all the marigolds. Avni and Kashish cornered Keshav by the handpump. "You were near the gate, na? You saw Raju open it, didn't you? He had his red cap on, na?" Keshav, nine, had been feeding tiffin crumbs to the sparrows. He hadn't seen anything. But the girls kept asking, closer and closer, and a picture came: a red cap, a hand on the latch. By afternoon he told the headmaster, "Raju opened it. He had his red cap." Raju burst into tears; he'd been absent that morning. The headmaster sat Keshav down on the verandah. "Tell me only what you saw yourself, from the start." Keshav was quiet a long time. "Sparrows," he said. "I saw sparrows."

qa.q: What had the headmaster's goat eaten?
qa.a: All the marigolds.

qa.q: Why did Keshav come to believe he saw Raju's red cap?
qa.a: Keshav felt pressured as Avni and Kashish kept asking leading questions about the cap and the latch, until the picture they described slowly became his own.

qa.q: What did the headmaster do that brought out the truth?
qa.a: He asked Keshav to tell only what he had seen himself, from the start, an open question that didn't suggest any answer.

qa.q: What was it like for Raju to be blamed?
qa.a: Raju was hurt and frightened, accused of something he couldn't have done since he was absent that morning.

grounding: A boy pressed with leading questions by classmates takes on a detail he never saw, until an open question brings back his own memory.

passage: After Saturday practice in Soweto, the clubhouse window was found cracked. Coach Zanele crouched in front of Omar, ten, who had been packing the cones. "You saw the older boys from the other club kicking balls at it, didn't you? Hard kicks, near the window?" Omar hesitated. He had seen balls, somewhere. "I think so." "The tall one in the green bib?" "...Yes. The green bib." By Monday Omar was telling his mother the whole scene: the tall boy, the crack, the laughing. His mother listened, then asked, "What did you see with your own eyes, before Coach asked you?" Omar opened his mouth and closed it. "I was packing cones. I heard a bang. That's all." He looked at the floor. "But the green bib feels real, Ma."

qa.q: What was Omar doing after practice?
qa.a: Packing the cones.

qa.q: How does Omar feel when his mother asks what he saw himself, and what shows it?
qa.a: Omar feels confused and uncomfortable, looking at the floor after admitting he only heard a bang, yet saying the green bib still feels real.

qa.q: Which question from Omar's mother helped, and why?
qa.a: "What did you see with your own eyes, before Coach asked you?" It was open and neutral, helping Omar separate what he saw from what was suggested.

qa.q: How might the tall boy in the green bib be affected if Omar's first story were believed?
qa.a: He could be blamed and punished for a window he may never have touched, all because of a suggested detail.

grounding: A boy questioned with leading words by his coach adopts details he never saw, until his mother asks an open question.

passage:
Tuesday
Today Ma'am asked me about the fight near the swings at lunch. She said, "Anand, you saw Karan push Jasleen first, didn't you?" I hadn't really seen the start. I was tying my shoe. But she said it like it was true, so I said, "Yes." Then she asked, "And he pushed her hard, right?" I said yes again, and I could almost see it in my head.
After school Jasleen told me Karan hadn't pushed her at all. They both slipped on the wet sand and bumped into each other. Now I feel terrible. Karan got a warning because of me. And the weird thing is, the push still feels like something I saw.
Tomorrow I'm going to tell Ma'am I was tying my shoe. Mummy said she'll come with me.
Anand

qa.q: What was Anand doing when the fight started?
qa.a: Anand was tying a shoe.

qa.q: Why does Anand feel terrible tonight?
qa.a: Anand feels guilty and confused, because agreeing with Ma'am's leading questions got Karan a warning, and now the push even feels like something Anand saw.

qa.q: What could Ma'am have asked instead, and what is Anand planning?
qa.a: She could have asked an open question like 'What did you see?'; Anand plans to tell her tomorrow, with Mummy there, about tying a shoe.

qa.q: How might Karan feel about the warning?
qa.a: Karan probably feels it was unfair, since he and Jasleen only slipped on the wet sand.

grounding: Shows a child adopting details from an adult's leading questions and coming to half-remember a push that never happened.

passage: When the goats got into Baljeet's wheat field in Rampur, Baljeet stormed round the lane asking questions. He stopped Asif, ten, by the well. "You saw the Verma boy open the gate, didn't you? The one in the red shirt?" Asif had only seen goats running. But Baljeet's face was so sure that he nodded. "Red shirt, yes." By evening, Asif was telling his friends about the red shirt himself. That night his Dada asked him quietly, "What did you actually see, from the very start?" Asif thought. Goats. Dust. Baljeet shouting. No boy. No red shirt. His stomach turned over. The next morning Dada walked with him to Baljeet's house, and Asif said he hadn't seen anyone open the gate.

qa.q: Where did Baljeet stop Asif?
qa.a: By the well.

qa.q: Why did Asif nod about the red shirt?
qa.a: Asif felt pressured and unsure, and Baljeet's certain question made agreeing feel easier, until the red shirt started to feel real.

qa.q: Why did Dada's question work better than Baljeet's?
qa.a: Dada asked an open question, what did you actually see from the start, which let Asif separate what he saw from what he was told.

qa.q: How might the Verma boy have been affected if Asif hadn't corrected himself?
qa.a: The Verma boy could have been blamed for something no one actually saw him do.

grounding: Shows a child adopting a detail from an adult's leading question, and an open question helping him recall what he really saw.

passage: In the courtyard of their building in Lisbon, Mr Costa found a long scratch on his car and came looking for witnesses. He found Noa, nine, and her friend Mateo on the steps. "You saw the boy with the blue bike do this, didn't you?" he asked Noa. "He was racing around, wasn't he?" Noa had been reading all afternoon. But Mr Costa sounded so sure, and the blue-bike boy did race around a lot. "I think so," she said. Mateo looked at her, surprised. Later, telling her mother, Noa added that the boy had laughed as he scraped it. Her mother frowned. "Tell me what you saw, from the beginning. Only what you saw." Noa opened her mouth and found only her book. "Nothing," she whispered. Her mother went with her to tell Mr Costa.

qa.q: What had Noa been doing all afternoon?
qa.a: Reading.

qa.q: How did Noa feel when she could remember only her book?
qa.a: Noa felt shaken and ashamed, realising the scratching and laughing had come from Mr Costa's questions, not from anything she saw.

qa.q: What made Noa's mother's question better than Mr Costa's?
qa.a: It was open and neutral, asking only what Noa saw from the beginning, without suggesting any answer.

qa.q: Why might Mateo have looked surprised?
qa.a: Mateo knew Noa had been reading all afternoon, so hearing her agree seemed strange.

grounding: Shows a child adopting details from a neighbour's leading questions until an open question reveals she saw nothing.

passage:
In the school's sports room, a cricket bat had been found cracked. The PE teacher gathered three boys, including Yogesh, ten.

"Yogesh, you saw Uday throw the bat against the wall, didn't you?"

Yogesh hesitated. He had been tying his laces. "I... heard a bang."

"A bang when Uday threw it?"

"Maybe... yes?"

"And then he laughed?"

"I think so."

Uday's face went red. "I didn't!"

The class teacher walked in. "Yogesh, just tell me what you saw. Nothing else."

Yogesh looked at the floor. "I didn't see anything. I only heard a bang. I was tying my laces."

The class teacher nodded. "Thank you. That's what matters."

qa.q: What was Yogesh doing when the bang happened?
qa.a: He was tying his laces.

qa.q: How did Yogesh probably feel when the PE teacher kept asking about Uday?
qa.a: He probably felt pressured and confused, as if he had to agree with what the teacher already believed.

qa.q: What did the class teacher do differently, and why did it help?
qa.a: The class teacher asked Yogesh to say only what he saw, an open question, which let him give an honest answer.

qa.q: How might Uday have felt hearing Yogesh agree at first?
qa.a: Uday was probably scared and angry, being blamed for something by a friend who hadn't seen it.

grounding: A child questioned with leading words starts to agree to details that weren't true, until an open question lets him answer honestly.

passage:
Monday. Pradeep's lunchbox went missing. His classmate Eshaan asked, "Did you see Rohit take it? He was near your bag, right?" Pradeep, nine, had not seen anything, but he said, "Maybe."

Wednesday. Eshaan and others kept asking. "Rohit took it, na? He looked guilty?" Pradeep started to remember Rohit near his bag, smiling. He told his teacher Rohit took it.

Friday. The lunchbox was found under the bench in the music room, where Pradeep had left it. Rohit looked hurt. Pradeep felt awful.

His teacher sat with him. "Next time, just say what you saw. It's okay to say you don't know." Pradeep nodded, and went to say sorry to Rohit.

qa.q: Where was the lunchbox found?
qa.a: Under the bench in the music room.

qa.q: Why did Pradeep start to remember Rohit near his bag?
qa.a: The repeated questions made Pradeep feel pressured, and the suggested picture slowly felt like a real memory.

qa.q: What small step did the teacher suggest, and why does it matter?
qa.a: The teacher said to share only what he saw and that it's fine to say "I don't know," which protects him from false details.

qa.q: What was it like for Rohit to be blamed?
qa.a: Rohit felt hurt, being accused of something he didn't do.

grounding: A child questioned with leading words by peers adopts a false detail about a missing lunchbox, and learns to say only what he saw.

passage:
Francis, you're asking why I'm careful when I ask children questions at the school? Let your Karthik uncle tell you about when I was eight.

A window in our lane got broken. The neighbour came to me and said, "You saw the Sharma boy throw the stone, didn't you? A big stone?" I hadn't seen anything. But she asked again, "A big stone, yes?" I nodded, because she was an adult and she seemed sure.

By evening I was telling my mother about the stone. I could almost see it.

The next day the Sharma boy was punished. Later we found out a ball had hit the window during cricket.

I felt sick. Now, when I talk to children, I only ask, "What did you see?" Then I listen.

qa.q: What actually broke the window?
qa.a: A ball had hit the window during cricket.

qa.q: Why did young Karthik nod when the neighbour asked about the stone?
qa.a: He felt small and unsure, and because an adult seemed so sure, agreeing felt like the right answer.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how Karthik asks questions?
qa.a: Finding out the ball broke the window, and that the Sharma boy was punished wrongly, made him start asking only "What did you see?"

qa.q: How might the Sharma boy have felt when he was punished?
qa.a: He probably felt angry and hurt, being punished for something he didn't do.

grounding: An elder recalls how, as a child, leading questions made him adopt false details, and why open questions matter.

passage: The summer camp ground was baking hot, and the coach had ten minutes before the bus came. The clubhouse window was smashed. "Tejas, you saw Jomon throw the ball hard at the window, didn't you?" the coach said. "He was being careless, right?" Tejas had been drinking water behind the shed. He had only heard the crash. But the coach was waiting, the other boys were staring, and Tejas nodded. "Yes... he threw it hard." By the time the bus honked, Tejas was describing Jomon's red cap and the ball's curve. That evening his older sister asked him, "What did you actually see?" Tejas went quiet. "Only the glass on the ground," he said slowly.

qa.q: Where was Tejas when the window broke?
qa.a: Drinking water behind the shed.

qa.q: Why did Tejas agree with the coach?
qa.a: He felt pressured and nervous, with the coach waiting and the boys staring, so the leading question made agreeing feel right, and the extra details filled themselves in.

qa.q: How could the coach have asked in a fairer way?
qa.a: Ask an open question like "What did you see?" without naming Jomon, and give Tejas time away from the watching boys.

qa.q: How might Jomon be affected?
qa.a: Jomon could be blamed on the strength of details Tejas never saw, which is unfair and could hurt their friendship.

grounding: A boy given leading questions under time pressure adopts details he never saw, and an open question later brings out the truth.

passage: On Holi afternoon in their Pune colony, Mrs Kulkarni's white sheets on the balcony were streaked pink. She marched down to the children. "Dhruv, it was that tall boy Amandeep with the green bucket, wasn't it? You saw him laughing?" Dhruv had been busy chasing his cousin. But Mrs Kulkarni's voice was sharp, and her questions seemed to know the answer already. "I think... yes, a green bucket," he said. Soon he added that Amandeep had laughed. Later, while scrubbing colour off his arms, Dhruv's father asked plainly, "Tell me what you saw, from the start." Dhruv thought hard. "I didn't see the sheets at all," he admitted, ears hot.

qa.q: What colour were the streaks on Mrs Kulkarni's sheets?
qa.a: Pink.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when he answered Mrs Kulkarni?
qa.a: He felt nervous and pressured by her sharp voice; her questions seemed to hold the answer already, so agreeing felt easier than saying he had not seen anything.

qa.q: What made the father's question work better?
qa.a: It was open and neutral, "Tell me what you saw, from the start", so Dhruv could find his own memory instead of borrowing hers.

qa.q: What would it be like for Amandeep if Dhruv's first answer were believed?
qa.a: Amandeep would be blamed for something nobody saw him do, and might feel wronged and angry.

grounding: A boy agrees to details in an adult's leading questions, and an open question later brings back his accurate account.

passage:
"Manoj, you were in the store room during winter-break practice, right?" Darshan leaned in, breath steaming in the cold corridor. "Did you hear the cupboard door bang by itself?"
"I... there was a noise."
"A bang, right? And a cold wind, like someone walked past?"
"Maybe a wind," Manoj said. "It was cold everywhere."
"And a shadow near the window?"
"I think... yes, a shadow."
Two boys gasped. By lunch Manoj was saying the door had slammed three times.
Ms Fernandes, overhearing, crouched beside him. "Manoj, tell me what you remember, in your own words."
He paused. "I was getting chalk. I heard something fall. That's all, ma'am."
"Thank you. That's very clear."

qa.q: How many times did Manoj say the door had slammed, by lunch?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: Why did Manoj agree there was a shadow?
qa.a: He was unsure about the noise and probably wanted to match Darshan's excitement, so each leading question made the new detail feel right.

qa.q: What helped Manoj get back to what really happened?
qa.a: Ms Fernandes asked an open question, "tell me what you remember, in your own words", without suggesting a bang or a shadow.

qa.q: How might Darshan see those questions?
qa.a: Darshan probably saw the questions as curious fun, not noticing that they were feeding Manoj the story.

grounding: Peers' leading questions add a bang and a shadow to a boy's memory until an open question brings back the plain facts.

passage:
This happened in winter sports week. I'm Akash, and I'm in Class 5.
A ball smashed the staffroom window. Mr Rao came running and gripped my shoulder. "You saw Pema kick it, didn't you? That big red ball?"
I hadn't seen anything. I only heard the crash. But he looked so sure, and everyone was staring. "Yes," I said. "Red."
Then Priya said, "Pema kicked it really hard, right, Akash?" and I nodded. By lunch I could almost see Pema's foot.
The next day the principal called me in. She just asked, "What did you see or hear?" and waited. I sat for a long time. Then I said, "I heard a crash. That's all." My stomach felt better after that.
Pema was never punished.

qa.q: What did Akash actually hear?
qa.a: Akash only heard the crash.

qa.q: Why did Akash say "Yes" to Mr Rao?
qa.a: Mr Rao looked so sure and everyone was staring, so Akash felt scared and pressured into agreeing, and by lunch the suggested picture almost felt real.

qa.q: What did the principal do differently, and why did it help?
qa.a: She asked an open question, "What did you see or hear?", and waited, so Akash could separate what really happened from the suggested details.

qa.q: What might have happened to Pema if the principal had asked a leading question too?
qa.a: Pema might have been punished for something nobody actually saw, just because a suggested detail had spread.

grounding: Shows a child adopting untrue details under leading questions from an adult and classmates, and an open question protecting what is said.
